claim: Biomineralization had apparently evolved independently in different phyla, using distinct minerals, organic scaffolds, and gene regulatory networks (GRNs).
source: Biomineralization had apparently evolved independently in different phyla, using distinct minerals, organic scaffolds, and gene regulatory networks (GRNs).
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary history of biomineralization that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Diverse eukaryotes from unicellular organisms, through echinoderms to vertebrates, use the actomyosin network during biomineralization.
source: However, diverse eukaryotes from unicellular organisms, through echinoderms to vertebrates, use the actomyosin network during biomineralization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to various studies showing actomyosin involvement across different organisms.

claim: The actomyosin remodeling protein, Rho-associated coiled-coil kinase (ROCK) regulates cell differentiation and gene expression in vertebrates' biomineralizing cells.
source: Specifically, the actomyosin remodeling protein, Rho-associated coiled-coil kinase (ROCK) regulates cell differentiation and gene expression in vertebrates' biomineralizing cells, yet, little is known on ROCK's role in invertebrates' biomineralization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on ROCK in vertebrate biomineralization.

claim: ROCK expression is elevated in the sea urchin skeletogenic cells downstream of the Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) signaling.
source: ROCK expression is elevated in the sea urchin skeletogenic cells downstream of the Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 demonstrating ROCK enrichment in skeletogenic cells and its dependence on VEGF signaling.

claim: ROCK inhibition leads to skeletal loss and disrupts skeletogenic gene expression.
source: ROCK inhibition leads to skeletal loss and disrupts skeletogenic gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 7 showing skeletal phenotypes and gene expression changes under ROCK inhibition.

claim: ROCK inhibition after spicule formation reduces the spicule elongation rate and induces ectopic spicule branching.
source: ROCK inhibition after spicule formation reduces the spicule elongation rate and induces ectopic spicule branching.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3 showing reduced growth and branching phenotypes.

claim: Similar skeletogenic phenotypes are observed when ROCK is inhibited in a skeletogenic cell culture, indicating that these phenotypes are due to ROCK activity specifically in the skeletogenic cells.
source: Similar skeletogenic phenotypes are observed when ROCK is inhibited in a skeletogenic cell culture, indicating that these phenotypes are due to ROCK activity specifically in the skeletogenic cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from isolated skeletogenic cell cultures shown in Figure 2L-P.

claim: Reduced skeletal growth and enhanced branching are also observed under direct perturbations of the actomyosin network.
source: Reduced skeletal growth and enhanced branching are also observed under direct perturbations of the actomyosin network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing effects of Latrunculin-A and Blebbistatin treatments.

claim: ROCK and the actomyosin machinery were employed independently, downstream of distinct GRNs, to regulate biomineral growth and morphology in Eukaryotes.
source: We propose that ROCK and the actomyosin machinery were employed independently, downstream of distinct GRNs, to regulate biomineral growth and morphology in Eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis based on the integration of findings from this study and prior knowledge about biomineralization across different phyla.

claim: Recent studies suggest that biomineralization evolved by the phylum-specific co-option of ancestral GRNs that drove the construction of distinct organic scaffolds.
source: Recent studies suggest that biomineralization evolved by the phylum-specific co-option of ancestral GRNs that drove the construction of distinct organic scaffolds (Gilbert et al., 2022; Ben-Tabou de-Leon, 2022; Morgulis et al., 2019; Murdock, 2020; Hojo et al., 2016; Fraser et al., 2009) and by the evolution of specialized sets of biomineralization proteins (Knoll, 2003; Murdock, 2020; Evans, 2019; Khor and Ettensohn, 2017; Kawasaki et al., 2009; Drake et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent literature on biomineralization evolution.

claim: The actomyosin network was shown to play a role in biomineralization in various Eukaryote models, from unicellular organisms to vertebrates' bones and teeth.
source: The actomyosin network was shown to play a role in biomineralization in various Eukaryote models, from unicellular organisms to vertebrates' bones and teeth (Langer et al., 2010; Durak et al., 2017; Tyszka et al., 2019; Tesson and Hildebrand, 2010a; Tesson and Hildebrand, 2010b; Strzelecka-Kiliszek et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies across different organisms.

claim: There is a tight association between actin filaments and the biomineralization compartment in diatoms.
source: There is a tight association between actin filaments and the biomineralization compartment in diatoms (Tesson and Hildebrand, 2010b) and a highly dynamic actin organization that forms the biomineralization compartment in foraminifera (Tyszka et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies on diatoms and foraminifera.

claim: Perturbations of actin polymerization result in severely deformed shells and inhibition of shell shedding in coccolithophores and diatoms.
source: Perturbations of actin polymerization result in severely deformed shells and inhibition of shell shedding in coccolithophores (Langer et al., 2010; Durak et al., 2017) and diatoms (Tesson and Hildebrand, 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on coccolithophores and diatoms.

claim: In vertebrates, Rho GTPases and ROCK, regulate chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and odontoblasts differentiation and affect gene expression in these biomineralizing cells.
source: In vertebrates, Rho GTPases and ROCK, regulate chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and odontoblasts differentiation and affect gene expression in these biomineralizing cells (Strzelecka-Kiliszek et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on vertebrate biomineralizing cells.

claim: Sea urchin larval skeletons are made of two frameworks of interconnected calcite rods, termed 'spicules' that are generated by the skeletogenic cells.
source: Sea urchin larval skeletons are made of two frameworks of interconnected calcite rods, termed 'spicules' that are generated by the skeletogenic cells (Morgulis et al., 2019; Oliveri et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about sea urchin skeletogenesis supported by citations.

claim: To make the spicules, the skeletogenic cells form a ring with two lateral skeletogenic clusters and fuse through their filopodia forming a pseudopodia cable that links them into a syncytium.
source: To make the spicules, the skeletogenic cells form a ring with two lateral skeletogenic clusters and fuse through their filopodia forming a pseudopodia cable that links them into a syncytium (Ettensohn and Dey, 2017; Gildor et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing skeletogenic cell behavior.

claim: The mineral is concentrated in the form of amorphous calcium carbonate (ACC) inside intracellular vesicles.
source: The mineral is concentrated in the form of amorphous calcium carbonate (ACC) inside intracellular vesicles (Kahil et al., 2020; Kahil et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on mineral processing in sea urchin skeletogenesis.

claim: The vesicles are secreted into the biomineralization compartment generated in the skeletogenic cell clusters forming two triradiate spicules.
source: The vesicles are secreted into the biomineralization compartment generated in the skeletogenic cell clusters forming two triradiate spicules (Figure 8A, Kahil et al., 2020; Vidavsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 8A showing the process.

claim: The tubular biomineralization compartment, also called the spicule cavity, elongates within the pseudopodia cable by localized mineral deposition at the tip of each rod.
source: The tubular biomineralization compartment, also called the spicule cavity, elongates within the pseudopodia cable by localized mineral deposition at the tip of each rod (Wilt et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on spicule elongation.

claim: The GRN that controls sea urchin skeletogenesis is known in great detail and is highly similar to the GRN that controls vertebrates' vascularization, suggesting a common evolutionary origin of these two tubulogenesis programs.
source: The GRN that controls sea urchin skeletogenesis is known in great detail and is highly similar to the GRN that controls vertebrates' vascularization, suggesting a common evolutionary origin of these two tubulogenesis programs (Morgulis et al., 2019; Oliveri et al., 2008; Adomako-Ankomah and Ettensohn, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents an inference about evolutionary relationships.

claim: As the spicules elongate, the expression of key regulatory and biomineralization-related genes becomes restricted to the skeletogenic cells proximal to the growing tips, possibly to promote mineral deposition at these sites.
source: As the spicules elongate, the expression of key regulatory and biomineralization-related genes becomes restricted to the skeletogenic cells proximal to the growing tips, possibly to promote mineral deposition at these sites (Sun and Ettensohn, 2014; Tarsis et al., 2022; Morgulis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and includes a speculative element about the purpose of localized expression.

claim: Localized gene expression is regulated by signaling cues such as the VEGF signaling.
source: Localized gene expression is regulated by signaling cues such as the VEGF signaling (Adomako-Ankomah and Ettensohn, 2013; Sun and Ettensohn, 2014; Tarsis et al., 2022; Duloquin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on VEGF signaling in skeletogenesis.

claim: Calcium-bearing vesicles perform an active diffusion motion in the skeletogenic cells with a diffusion length that inversely correlates with the strength and activity of the actomyosin network.
source: Calcium-bearing vesicles perform an active diffusion motion in the skeletogenic cells with a diffusion length that inversely correlates with the strength and activity of the actomyosin network (Winter et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on vesicle dynamics.

claim: Actin filaments are formed around the spicule.
source: Actin filaments are formed around the spicule (Winter et al., 2021; Stepicheva et al., 2017) and F-actin signal is enriched at the tips of the growing skeletal rods in skeletogenic cell culture (Moreno et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing F-actin localization.

claim: F-actin signal is enriched at the tips of the growing skeletal rods in skeletogenic cell culture.
source: Actin filaments are formed around the spicule (Winter et al., 2021; Stepicheva et al., 2017) and F-actin signal is enriched at the tips of the growing skeletal rods in skeletogenic cell culture (Moreno et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on F-actin localization in culture.

claim: Genetic and pharmacological perturbations of the GTPase, CDC42, prevent the formation of filopodia in the skeletogenic cells and inhibit spicule formation and elongation.
source: Genetic and pharmacological perturbations of the GTPase, CDC42, prevent the formation of filopodia in the skeletogenic cells and inhibit spicule formation and elongation (Sepúlveda-Ramírez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on CDC42 in skeletogenesis.

claim: Pharmacological perturbations of ROCK prevent spicule formation.
source: Pharmacological perturbations of ROCK prevent spicule formation (Croce et al., 2006) and genetic perturbations of Rhogap24l/2 result in ectopic spicule splitting (Morgulis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on ROCK inhibition.

claim: Genetic perturbations of Rhogap24l/2 result in ectopic spicule splitting.
source: Pharmacological perturbations of ROCK prevent spicule formation (Croce et al., 2006) and genetic perturbations of Rhogap24l/2 result in ectopic spicule splitting (Morgulis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Rhogap24l/2.

claim: The sequence of ROCK and especially, its functional domains are highly conserved between human and sea urchin.
source: The sequence of ROCK and especially, its functional domains are highly conserved between human and sea urchin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Marlétaz et al., 2023; Arshinoff et al., 2022; Telmer et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to sequence databases.

claim: According to RNA-seq data measured in P. lividus, ROCK is a maternal gene that degrades after the maternal to zygotic transition and picks up again after hatching >14 hr post fertilization (hpf).
source: According to RNA-seq data measured in P. lividus, ROCK is a maternal gene that degrades after the maternal to zygotic transition and picks up again after hatching >14 hr post fertilization (hpf), (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The antibody detected a ~150 kDa protein that is the predicted size for P. lividus ROCK protein (153 kDa).
source: The antibody detected a ~150 kDa protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) that is the predicted size for P. lividus ROCK protein (153 kDa).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: VEGFR inhibition marginally increased the overall level of ROCK at 22hpf, but did not affect it at 27hpf and 33hpf.
source: VEGFR inhibition marginally increased the overall level of ROCK at 22hpf, but did not affect it at 27hpf and 33hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The skeletogenic cells, where VEGFR is active, are less than 5% of the total cell mass.
source: Yet, this measurement was done on proteins extracted from whole embryos, of which the skeletogenic cells, where VEGFR is active, are less than 5% of the total cell mass (Massri et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on cell composition.

claim: At 22hpf, ROCK expression in the skeletogenic cells is mildly enriched compared to the neighboring ectodermal cells, and this enrichment is not observed under VEGFR inhibition.
source: At 22hpf, ROCK expression in the skeletogenic cells is mildly enriched compared to the neighboring ectodermal cells, and this enrichment is not observed under VEGFR inhibition (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-F.

claim: At 27hpf, ROCK enrichment in the skeletogenic cells increases, but similar enrichment is observed under VEGFR inhibition.
source: At 27hpf, ROCK enrichment in the skeletogenic cells increases, but similar enrichment is observed under VEGFR inhibition (Figure 1G–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G-L.

claim: At 33hpf, ROCK enrichment in the skeletogenic cells is most apparent and depends on VEGF signaling.
source: At 33hpf, ROCK enrichment in the skeletogenic cells is most apparent (Figure 1M–O) and depends on VEGF signaling (Figure 1P-S).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1M-S.

claim: At both 27hpf and 33hpf in control embryos, ROCK seems localized near the skeletogenic cell membranes, which further supports its activation in these cells, since ROCK activation leads to its localization to the cell membranes in other systems.
source: At both 27hpf and 33hpf in control embryos, ROCK seems localized near the skeletogenic cell membranes, which further supports its activation in these cells, since ROCK activation leads to its localization to the cell membranes in other systems (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on observed localization patterns and comparison to known ROCK behavior in other systems.

claim: Embryos injected with either ROCK MASO-1 or MASO-2 show reduced ROCK signal at 33hpf, supporting the downregulation of the ROCK protein using these MASO's.
source: Embryos injected with either ROCK MASO-1 or MASO-2 show reduced ROCK signal at 33hpf, supporting the downregulation of the ROCK protein using these MASO's (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, F, J, N, R, V).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Embryos injected with ROCK MASO-1 or MASO-2 show strongly reduced skeletons at two days post fertilization (2dpf).
source: Embryos injected with ROCK MASO-1 or MASO-2 show strongly reduced skeletons at two days post fertilization (2dpf, Figure 2C and D) and embryos injected with ROCK MASO-2 show an additional phenotype of the severely branched skeleton at this time (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Embryos injected with ROCK MASO-2 show an additional phenotype of the severely branched skeleton at 2dpf.
source: Embryos injected with ROCK MASO-1 or MASO-2 show strongly reduced skeletons at two days post fertilization (2dpf, Figure 2C and D) and embryos injected with ROCK MASO-2 show an additional phenotype of the severely branched skeleton at this time (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The additional branching phenotype and the larger percentage of affected embryos in ROCK MASO-2 are probably due to its higher efficiency resulting from its more 5' location relative to the translation start codon.
source: The additional branching phenotype and the larger percentage of affected embryos in ROCK MASO-2 are probably due to its higher efficiency resulting from its more 5' location relative to the translation start codon (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of morpholino action and the observed phenotypic differences.

claim: Y27632 affinity to ROCK is 100 times higher than its affinity to other kinases, such as PKA and PKC.
source: Y27632 affinity to ROCK is 100 times higher than its affinity to other kinases, such as PKA and PKC (Narumiya et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Y27632 specificity.

claim: The amino-acids to which Y27632 binds, are conserved in the sea urchin ROCK protein, supporting its specific inhibition of this protein.
source: The amino-acids to which Y27632 binds, are conserved in the sea urchin ROCK protein, supporting its specific inhibition of this protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Continuous ROCK inhibition beginning at egg fertilization, resulted in significant skeletogenic phenotypes that are dose-dependent.
source: Continuous ROCK inhibition beginning at egg fertilization, resulted in significant skeletogenic phenotypes that are dose-dependent (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Continuous ROCK inhibition using 80 µM Y27632, did not affect skeletogenic cell migration but eliminated skeletal formation at 27hpf.
source: Continuous ROCK inhibition using 80 µM Y27632, did not affect skeletogenic cell migration but eliminated skeletal formation at 27hpf (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: At 2dpf, complete skeletal loss is detected under continuous ROCK inhibition in all concentrations, ranging from 15% of the embryos exposed to 10 µM to 67% of the embryos exposed to 80 µM Y27632.
source: At 2dpf, complete skeletal loss is detected under continuous ROCK inhibition in all concentrations, ranging from 15% of the embryos exposed to 10 µM to 67% of the embryos exposed to 80 µM Y27632 (Figure 2G and K, in agreement with Croce et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and K.

claim: Skeletal loss, spicule initiation, and ectopic branching were not observed under PKC or PKA inhibition, that resulted in much milder skeletogenic phenotypes (PKC) or no skeletogenic phenotype (PKA), supporting the selective inhibition of ROCK by Y27632.
source: Importantly, skeletal loss, spicule initiation, and ectopic branching were not observed under PKC or PKA inhibition, that resulted in much milder skeletogenic phenotypes (PKC) or no skeletogenic phenotype (PKA, Mitsunaga et al., 1990a; Mitsunaga et al., 1990b), supporting the selective inhibition of ROCK by Y27632.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to control experiments with other kinase inhibitors, cited from prior studies.

claim: The addition of the inhibitor at 25hpf, after spicule initiation, results in a majority of embryos showing ectopic spicule branching.
source: The addition of the inhibitor at 25hpf, after spicule initiation, results in a majority of embryos showing ectopic spicule branching (Figure 2H–K, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-H, K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H-K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The reduction of skeletal growth rate and ectopic branching can be observed a few hours after the addition of ROCK inhibitor.
source: The reduction of skeletal growth rate and ectopic branching can be observed a few hours after the addition of ROCK inhibitor (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, 30 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Washing the inhibitor at the highest concertation after 25hpf results in partial recovery of skeletogenesis, with normal or mildly delayed skeletons, indicating that ROCK inhibition is reversible.
source: Washing the inhibitor at the highest concertation after 25hpf results in partial recovery of skeletogenesis, with normal or mildly delayed skeletons, indicating that ROCK inhibition is reversible (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, K.

claim: The injected MASO's cannot interfere with the maternal ROCK protein whereas the inhibitor affects the activity of both maternal and zygotic ROCK, which could underlie the absence of skeletal loss in the genetic perturbations.
source: The injected MASO's cannot interfere with the maternal ROCK protein whereas the inhibitor affects the activity of both maternal and zygotic ROCK, which could underlie the absence of skeletal loss in the genetic perturbations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of morpholino action and the observed phenotypic differences between genetic and pharmacological perturbations.

claim: The addition of ROCK inhibitor to the skeletogenic cell culture at 16hpf, before the spicules form, completely abolished spicule formation.
source: The addition of ROCK inhibitor to the skeletogenic cell culture at 16hpf, before the spicules form, completely abolished spicule formation (Figure 2M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from skeletogenic cell culture shown in Figure 2M.

claim: The addition of the inhibitor at 48hpf, after spicule formation, resulted in significantly shorter spicules and increased branching compared to control spicules.
source: The addition of the inhibitor at 48hpf, after spicule formation, resulted in significantly shorter spicules (Figure 2L and N) and increased branching compared to control spicules (Figure 2O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from skeletogenic cell culture shown in Figure 2L, N, and O.

claim: The reduction of the spicule length becomes more significant with increasing concentration of the ROCK inhibitor.
source: The reduction of the spicule length becomes more significant with increasing concentration of the ROCK inhibitor (Figure 2P).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2P.

claim: Skeletal loss and ectopic spicule branching were not observed in PKA or PKC inhibition in skeletogenic cell cultures, further supporting the selective inhibition of ROCK by Y27632.
source: Notably, skeletal loss and ectopic spicule branching were not observed in PKA or PKC inhibition in skeletogenic cell cultures (Mitsunaga et al., 1990b), further supporting the selective inhibition of ROCK by Y27632.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to control experiments cited from prior studies.

claim: The aberrant morphology of ROCK-inhibited spicules is visible at both 2dpf and 3dpf developmental time points.
source: The aberrant morphology of ROCK-inhibited spicules is visible at both developmental time points (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SR-µCT imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ectopic branching occurs both at the tips where tip-splitting is detected, as well as in the back, where small spicule extensions, or mineral 'dripping' are observed.
source: The ectopic branching occurs both at the tips where tip-splitting is detected (arrowheads, Figure 3A), as well as in the back, where small spicule extensions, or mineral 'dripping' are observed (arrow at 48hpf, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SR-µCT imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The regulation of mineral deposition is perturbed both at the tip and in the back of the spicules under ROCK inhibition.
source: This demonstrates that the regulation of mineral deposition is perturbed both at the tip and in the back of the spicules under ROCK inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed branching patterns at both tips and back of spicules.

claim: ROCK inhibition leads to a ~2.5 fold reduction of the spicule volume and surface area in both 2 and 3dpf.
source: When compared to control spicules, ROCK inhibition leads to a ~2.5 fold reduction of the spicule volume and surface area in both 2 and 3dpf (Figure 3B–D, see Supplementary file 1b for measured values and standard deviations and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for statistical analyses).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative SR-µCT data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The average rate of spicule growth between 48hpf and 72hpf in control embryos is 325.5 µm3/hr, and reduces to 119.8 µm3/hr under ROCK inhibition.
source: The average rate of spicule growth between 48hpf and 72hpf in control embryos is 325.5 µm3/hr, and reduces to 119.8 µm3/hr under ROCK inhibition.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of SR-µCT data.

claim: The rate of mineral deposition is significantly reduced under ROCK inhibition.
source: Hence, the rate of mineral deposition is significantly reduced under ROCK inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured reduction in spicule growth rate.

claim: The total length of control spicules was on average about 2.5 times longer than the length under ROCK inhibition in both 2dpf and 3dpf.
source: The total length of control spicules was on average about 2.5 times longer than the length under ROCK inhibition in both 2dpf and 3dpf (Figure 3E and F, Supplementary file 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative SR-µCT data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: ROCK inhibition caused a minor increase of the spicule thickness at 2dpf, and at 3dpf the thickness was not affected by the inhibition.
source: In contrast to its effect on the spicule length, ROCK inhibition caused a minor increase of the spicule thickness at 2dpf, and at 3dpf the thickness was not affected by the inhibition (Figure 3E–G, Supplementary file 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative SR-µCT data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: ROCK activity plays a crucial role in controlling the rate of mineral deposition at the tips of the rods and spicule elongation, and is not affecting spicule thickening.
source: These SR-µCT measurements indicate that ROCK activity plays a crucial role in controlling the rate of mineral deposition at the tips of the rods and spicule elongation, and is not affecting spicule thickening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of ROCK inhibition on length versus thickness.

claim: Continuous ROCK inhibition does not change the number of calcium-bearing vesicles at 1dpf, but the number of calcein-stained pixels significantly increases in this condition, possibly indicating that the vesicle volume is larger.
source: Continuous ROCK inhibition does not change the number of calcium-bearing vesicles at 1dpf, but the number of calcein-stained pixels significantly increases in this condition, possibly indicating that the vesicle volume is larger (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative calcein staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, G.

claim: At 2dpf, the number of calcein-stained pixels is similar in control and in continuous ROCK inhibition, suggesting that the overall calcium content does not change in this condition.
source: At 2dpf, the number of calcein-stained pixels is similar in control and in continuous ROCK inhibition, suggesting that the overall calcium content does not change in this condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative calcein staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H, I.

claim: Addition of ROCK inhibitor at 25hpf affects neither the number of calcein-stained vesicles nor the number of calcein-stained pixels in the skeletogenic cells.
source: Addition of ROCK inhibitor at 25hpf affects neither the number of calcein-stained vesicles nor the number of calcein-stained pixels in the skeletogenic cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative calcein staining data.

claim: ROCK is not required for the uptake of calcium into the cells.
source: Together, these measurements show that ROCK is not required for the uptake of calcium into the cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcein staining data showing no reduction in calcium content.

claim: The skeletal phenotypes occurring under ROCK inhibition are not related to a decrease in calcium uptake or shortage in intracellular calcium, but are due to defects in mineral processing within the cells and in the mineral deposition.
source: Therefore, the skeletal phenotypes occurring under ROCK inhibition are not related to a decrease in calcium uptake or shortage in intracellular calcium, but are due to defects in mineral processing within the cells and in the mineral deposition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcein staining data and observed skeletal phenotypes.

claim: Under ROCK inhibition, the green labeled region is much closer to the blue labeled region compared to the control, due to the reduction in skeletal elongation rate.
source: Under ROCK inhibition, the green labeled region is much closer to the blue labeled region compared to the control, due to the reduction in skeletal elongation rate, in agreement with our SR-µCT measurements.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-pulse calcein labeling data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: While in control embryos each body rod has a single tip stained in green calcein, under ROCK inhibition one of the body rods has two tips and both are stained in green.
source: However, while in control embryos each body rod has a single tip stained in green calcein, under ROCK inhibition one of the body rods has two tips and both are stained in green.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-pulse calcein labeling data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: Mineral is being deposited in both edges under ROCK inhibition, and the mechanism that prevents the growth of multiple tips in each rod, enabling 'tip-dominance,' is disrupted under ROCK inhibition.
source: This indicates that mineral is being deposited in both edges, and the mechanism that prevents the growth of multiple tips in each rod, enabling 'tip-dominance,' (in analogy to plant stem apical dominance), is disrupted under ROCK inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the two-pulse calcein labeling data showing mineral deposition at multiple tips.

claim: The major roles of ROCK are to control F-actin polymerization and MyoII activation.
source: In other systems, the major roles of ROCK are to control F-actin polymerization and MyoII activation (Liu et al., 2018; Julian and Olson, 2014; Lecuit et al., 2011; Amin et al., 2013; Pavlov et al., 2007), hence we wanted to directly test the role of these actomyosin components in sea urchin skeletogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on ROCK function in other systems.

claim: The majority of the embryos where MyoII activation was inhibited show ectopic branching mostly at the tips of the rods, and a minor delay in skeletal growth.
source: The majority of the embryos where MyoII activation was inhibited show ectopic branching mostly at the tips of the rods, and a minor delay in skeletal growth (Figure 4B, C and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on Blebbistatin treatment shown in Figure 4B, C and G.

claim: The majority of the embryos where F-actin formation was inhibited show a significant reduction of skeletal growth and severe ectopic skeletal branching.
source: The majority of the embryos where F-actin formation was inhibited show a significant reduction of skeletal growth and severe ectopic skeletal branching (Figure 4E and F and similar phenotypes to Figure 4D, statistics in Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on Latrunculin-A treatment shown in Figure 4E, F and G.

claim: The co-inhibition of F-actin polymerization and MyoII activity results in skeletogenic phenotypes that resemble, but are slightly stronger, than those of the inhibition of F-actin alone.
source: The co-inhibition of F-actin polymerization and MyoII activity results in skeletogenic phenotypes that resemble, but are slightly stronger, than those of the inhibition of F-actin alone (Figure 4D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on combined treatment shown in Figure 4D and G.

claim: Both inhibitors reduced skeletal growth, with Lantruculin-A having a significantly stronger effect than Blebbistatin.
source: Both inhibitors reduced skeletal growth, with Lantruculin-A having a significantly stronger effect than Blebbistatin (Figure 4K), in agreement with the stronger skeletogenic phenotypes of Lantruculin-A in whole embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from skeletogenic cell culture shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Differently than in whole embryos, skeletal branching in both Lantruculin-A and Blebbistatin is not affected and is similar to the observed branching in control cultures.
source: However, differently than in whole embryos, skeletal branching in both Lantruculin-A and Blebbistatin is not affected and is similar to the observed branching in control cultures.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from skeletogenic cell culture experiments.

claim: The absence of the branching phenotype in the skeletogenic cell culture could be due to the increased rigidity of the substrate that could compensate for the reduced actomyosin activity.
source: The absence of the branching phenotype in the skeletogenic cell culture could be due to the increased rigidity of the substrate that could compensate for the reduced actomyosin activity.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference between whole embryos and cell culture.

claim: Another option is that the branching phenotype in whole embryos is due to the reduction of the activity of the actomyosin network in non-skeletogenic cells.
source: Another option is that the branching phenotype in whole embryos is due to the reduction of the activity of the actomyosin network in non-skeletogenic cells.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative explanation for the observed difference.

claim: Normal skeletal growth depends primarily on F-actin polymerization and to a lesser extent, on myosin contractility in the skeletogenic cells.
source: Nevertheless, these results indicate that normal skeletal growth depends primarily on F-actin polymerization and to a lesser extent, on myosin contractility in the skeletogenic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of Latrunculin-A and Blebbistatin in cell culture.

claim: In control embryos, F-actin is detected around the tri-radiate calcite spicules at 27hpf.
source: In control embryos, F-actin is detected around the tri-radiate calcite spicules at 27hpf (green arrow in Figure 5B, in agreement with Winter et al., 2021; Stepicheva et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 5B and citations to prior studies.

claim: The pseudopodia cable that connects the skeletogenic cells shows a lower F-actin signal compared to the signal around the spicule.
source: The pseudopodia cable that connects the skeletogenic cells shows a lower F-actin signal compared to the signal around the spicule (blue line in Figure 5B, C and E blue arrows in Figure 5G, H and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MyoIIP signal is not enriched in the skeletogenic cells nor in the spicule at 27hpf.
source: MyoIIP signal is not enriched in the skeletogenic cells nor in the spicule (Figure 5D I).
evidence: This claim is supported by MyoIIP immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D and I.

claim: Under continuous ROCK inhibition, the pseudopodia that connects the skeletogenic cells still forms.
source: Under continuous ROCK inhibition, the pseudopodia that connects the skeletogenic cells still forms (Figure 5R), and an enhanced F-actin signal is still observed in the lateral skeletogenic cell clusters (green arrow in Figure 5L); but unlike control embryos, the spicule cavity is not formed and F-actin is not organized around it (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 5R.

claim: Under continuous ROCK inhibition, an enhanced F-actin signal is still observed in the lateral skeletogenic cell clusters; but unlike control embryos, the spicule cavity is not formed and F-actin is not organized around it.
source: Under continuous ROCK inhibition, the pseudopodia that connects the skeletogenic cells still forms (Figure 5R), and an enhanced F-actin signal is still observed in the lateral skeletogenic cell clusters (green arrow in Figure 5L); but unlike control embryos, the spicule cavity is not formed and F-actin is not organized around it (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: MyoIIP signal seems unchanged by ROCK inhibition at 27hpf.
source: MyoIIP signal seems unchanged by ROCK inhibition at this time (Figure 5N and S), in agreement with the weak and late phenotype of MyoII inhibition (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by MyoIIP immunostaining data shown in Figure 5N and S.

claim: The pseudopodia cable forms but F-actin organization around the spicules does not occur under continuous ROCK inhibition.
source: Thus, the pseudopodia cable forms but F-actin organization around the spicules does not occur under continuous ROCK inhibition, however, it is not clear if the effect on F-actin organization is direct or due to the absence of spicule in this condition.
evidence: This is a summary statement with a caveat about interpretation.

claim: In both control and ROCK-inhibited embryos, the F-actin signal was markedly higher in the regions of the pseudopodia cable where the spicule cavity had formed, compared to the regions where the spicule cavity had not yet formed.
source: In both control and ROCK-inhibited embryos, the F-actin signal was markedly higher in the regions of the pseudopodia cable where the spicule cavity had formed, compared to the regions where the spicule cavity had not yet formed (blue arrows in Figure 6B–E and G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 6B-E and G-J.

claim: The phalloidin signal is on average threefold stronger at the tips of the spicules compared to the back, in both control and ROCK inhibition, indicating that F-actin enrichment at the tips is significant and independent of ROCK activity.
source: The phalloidin signal is on average threefold stronger at the tips of the spicules compared to the back, in both control and ROCK inhibition, indicating that F-actin enrichment at the tips is significant and independent of ROCK activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of phalloidin signal shown in Figure 6K and L.

claim: At the pluteus stage, F-actin is enriched at the tips of the spicules in both control and ROCK-inhibited embryos.
source: At the pluteus stage, F-actin is enriched at the tips of the spicules in both control and ROCK-inhibited embryos (white arrowheads in Figure 6N–Q)(Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 6N-Q.

claim: F-actin coats the spicule cavity and is enriched at the tip of the rods, independently of ROCK activity.
source: Together these data demonstrate that F-actin coats the spicule cavity and is enriched at the tip of the rods, independently of ROCK activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the phalloidin staining data across multiple timepoints.

claim: F-actin is detected at the tips, in both control cultures and cultures where ROCK was inhibited after spicule formation.
source: F-actin is detected at the tips, in both control cultures and cultures where ROCK was inhibited after spicule formation (Figure 6W X).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data from skeletogenic cell culture shown in Figure 6W and X.

claim: Under ROCK inhibition, branching is enhanced and F-actin is enriched at the splitting tips of the spicule rods.
source: Yet, under ROCK inhibition, branching is enhanced and F-actin is enriched at the splitting tips of the spicule rods (Fig, 6 X).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining data from skeletogenic cell culture shown in Figure 6X.

claim: The enrichment of F-actin at the splitting tips of the spicule under ROCK inhibition in skeletogenic cell culture resembles the calcein staining at the two tips in the embryo in this condition.
source: The enrichment of F-actin at the splitting tips of the spicule under ROCK inhibition in skeletogenic cell culture resembles the calcein staining at the two tips in the embryo in this condition (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a comparison between observations from cell culture and whole embryos.

claim: ROCK continuous inhibition significantly downregulates the expression of multiple skeletogenic genes, including the cytoskeleton remodeling gene, rhogap24l/2, the biomineralization genes, caral7, scl26a5, and SM30 at 27hpf and 2dpf.
source: ROCK continuous inhibition significantly downregulates the expression of multiple skeletogenic genes, including the cytoskeleton remodeling gene, rhogap24l/2, the biomineralization genes, caral7, scl26a5, and SM30 at 27hpf and 2dpf (Figure 7A, Morgulis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ROCK inhibition did not affect the expression level of VEGFR and ROCK itself at 27hpf and 2dpf.
source: ROCK inhibition did not affect the expression level of VEGFR and ROCK itself at these times (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Washing the inhibitor after 25hpf or adding the inhibitor at 25hpf had a weaker effect, but still led to downregulation of caral7, SM30, angio1, and notch1.
source: Washing the inhibitor after 25hpf or adding the inhibitor at 25hpf had a weaker effect, but still led to downregulation of caral7, SM30, angio1, and notch1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ROCK activity is required for the normal expression level of multiple skeletogenic genes during sea urchin skeletogenesis.
source: Thus, ROCK activity is required for the normal expression level of multiple skeletogenic genes during sea urchin skeletogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the qPCR data.

claim: Both continuous and late ROCK inhibition strongly affect the spatial expression of key regulatory and biomineralization genes that are normally expressed differentially within the skeletogenic lineage at the pluteus stage.
source: Both continuous and late ROCK inhibition strongly affect the spatial expression of key regulatory and biomineralization genes that are normally expressed differentially within the skeletogenic lineage at the pluteus stage (Figure 7D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7D-F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In both continuous and late ROCK inhibition the expression of these genes becomes localized to the two lateral skeletogenic cell clusters and their vicinity.
source: In both continuous and late ROCK inhibition the expression of these genes becomes localized to the two lateral skeletogenic cell clusters and their vicinity (Figure 7D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7D-F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lateral skeletogenic cell clusters are the cells where these genes are expressed in the gastrula stage (24-27hpf) and where spicule formation begins in normal embryos.
source: The lateral skeletogenic cell clusters are the cells where these genes are expressed in the gastrula stage (24-27hpf) and where spicule formation begins in normal embryos (Morgulis et al., 2019; Tarsis et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on gene expression patterns.

claim: The expression of VEGFR and SM50 under ROCK inhibition is more expanded than the other tested genes and is also observed at the anterolateral rods.
source: The expression of VEGFR and SM50 under ROCK inhibition is more expanded than the other tested genes and is also observed at the anterolateral rods (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The VEGF ligand that is normally expressed in the ectodermal cells near the four tips of the post-oral and anterolateral rods, is expressed at four ectodermal domains near the lateral skeletogenic cell clusters and near the end of the anterolateral chain, under ROCK inhibition.
source: The VEGF ligand that is normally expressed in the ectodermal cells near the four tips of the post-oral and anterolateral rods (Tarsis et al., 2022), is expressed at four ectodermal domains near the lateral skeletogenic cell clusters and near the end of the anterolateral chain, under ROCK inhibition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under ROCK inhibition, the expression of key skeletogenic genes remains localized to the area near the lateral skeletogenic cell clusters, despite the proper formation of the dorsal, anterolateral and mid-ventral chains.
source: Our data shows that under ROCK inhibition, the expression of key skeletogenic genes remains localized to the area near the lateral skeletogenic cell clusters (Figure 7D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), despite the proper formation of the dorsal, anterolateral and mid-ventral chains (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7C-F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ROCK activity is essential for normal expression level and spatial gene expression in the skeletogenic lineage.
source: Overall, ROCK activity is essential for normal expression level and spatial gene expression in the skeletogenic lineage.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the gene expression data.

claim: ROCK activity in the skeletogenic cells is necessary for spicule formation, skeletal elongation, and prevention of ectopic skeletal branching.
source: ROCK activity in the skeletogenic cells is necessary for spicule formation, skeletal elongation, and prevention of ectopic skeletal branching (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple experimental results.

claim: Direct inhibition of F-actin polymerization results in similar but not identical skeletogenic phenotypes.
source: Direct inhibition of F-actin polymerization results in similar but not identical skeletogenic phenotypes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on Latrunculin-A experiments.

claim: ROCK activity feeds back into the skeletogenic GRN and affects regulatory and biomineralization gene expression.
source: ROCK activity feeds back into the skeletogenic GRN and affects regulatory and biomineralization gene expression (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on gene expression data.

claim: The first step in generating the sea urchin spicules is the construction of the spicule cavity where the mineral is engulfed in a membrane coated with F-actin.
source: The first step in generating the sea urchin spicules is the construction of the spicule cavity where the mineral is engulfed in a membrane coated with F-actin (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the spicule formation process.

claim: ROCK activity is necessary for the spicule initiation and for the organization of F-actin around the spicule cavity.
source: ROCK activity is necessary for the spicule initiation and for the organization of F-actin around the spicule cavity (Figures 2, 5 and 8B).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on experimental results.

claim: A direct perturbation of F-actin polymerization strongly disrupts spicule growth and shape, but not spicule formation, indicating that F-actin is not essential for spicule initiation.
source: Relatedly, a direct perturbation of F-actin polymerization strongly disrupts spicule growth and shape, but not spicule formation, indicating that F-actin is not essential for spicule initiation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Latrunculin-A experiments.

claim: ROCK activity is necessary for spicule initiation, but not through its' direct regulation of the actomyosin network, but though its other targets, yet to be identified.
source: We, therefore, propose that ROCK activity is necessary for spicule initiation, but not through its' direct regulation of the actomyosin network, but though its other targets, yet to be identified (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis based on the integration of experimental results.

claim: After the spicule cavity has formed, the spicules elongate inside the pseudopodia chord by mineral deposition at the tips of the spicule rods, which depends on ROCK activity, on F-actin polymerization, and to a lesser extent, on MyoII contractility.
source: After the spicule cavity has formed, the spicules elongate inside the pseudopodia chord by mineral deposition at the tips of the spicule rods, which depends on ROCK activity, on F-actin polymerization, and to a lesser extent, on MyoII contractility (Figures 2—4 and 8D–F).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple experimental results.

claim: The low dosage of late ROCK inhibition is perturbing mostly ROCK activation of MyoII contractility while the higher dosage affects factors that control actin polymerization.
source: These correlative similarities between ROCK and the actomyosin perturbations lead us to the following speculations: the low dosage of late ROCK inhibition is perturbing mostly ROCK activation of MyoII contractility while the higher dosage affects factors that control actin polymerization (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the dose-dependent effects.

claim: The participation of ROCK, F-actin, and MyoII in polarized growth and vesicle exocytosis has been observed in both animals and plants.
source: The participation of ROCK, F-actin, and MyoII in polarized growth and vesicle exocytosis has been observed in both animals and plants (Miklavc and Frick, 2020; Bibeau et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on polarized growth and exocytosis.

claim: F-actin is used for short-range myosin trafficking of vesicles toward the secretion site.
source: F-actin is used for short-range myosin trafficking of vesicles toward the secretion site (Miklavc and Frick, 2020; Bond et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on vesicle trafficking.

claim: Once the secretory vesicle fuses with the membrane, it is coated with F-actin that stabilizes the vesicle and enables MyoII binding and ROCK-regulated contraction, necessary for content secretion.
source: Once the secretory vesicle fuses with the membrane, it is coated with F-actin that stabilizes the vesicle and enables MyoII binding and ROCK-regulated contraction, necessary for content secretion (Segal et al., 2018; Rousso et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on vesicle exocytosis.

claim: In plant cells, F-actin accumulates at the growing tip of the cell and assists in vesicle exocytosis necessary for polarized tip-growth.
source: In plant cells, F-actin accumulates at the growing tip of the cell and assists in vesicle exocytosis necessary for polarized tip-growth (Bibeau et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on plant cell growth.

claim: ROCK, F-actin, and MyoII could be regulating the localized exocytosis of mineral-bearing vesicles during sea urchin skeletogenesis.
source: ROCK, F-actin, and MyoII could be regulating the localized exocytosis of mineral-bearing vesicles during sea urchin skeletogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed roles of these factors in other systems.

claim: The reduction of spicule growth rate and the enhanced branching could be due to impaired and misplaced vesicle trafficking and deposition under ROCK and F-actin inhibition.
source: The reduction of spicule growth rate and the enhanced branching could be due to impaired and misplaced vesicle trafficking and deposition under ROCK and F-actin inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenotypes.

claim: ROCK activity provides regulatory cues to the skeletogenic GRN required for the dynamic progression of gene expression within the skeletogenic lineage.
source: This implies that ROCK activity provides regulatory cues to the skeletogenic GRN required for the dynamic progression of gene expression within the skeletogenic lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of ROCK inhibition on gene expression.

claim: ROCK activity was shown to regulate gene expression through various intracellular pathways.
source: In other systems, ROCK activity was shown to regulate gene expression through various intracellular pathways (Olson and Nordheim, 2010; Knipe et al., 2015; Khatiwala et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on ROCK signaling.

claim: ROCK has an important role in the mechano-sensing of matrix rigidity and transducing it into changes in gene expression.
source: Furthermore, ROCK has an important role in the mechano-sensing of matrix rigidity and transducing it into changes in gene expression (Zhong et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on mechanotransduction.

claim: Stiff substrate activates ROCK in pre-osteoblastic cells in-vitro, which activates Erk that leads to osteogenic differentiation and upregulation of osteogenic gene expression.
source: Relatedly, stiff substrate activates ROCK in pre-osteoblastic cells in-vitro, which activates Erk that leads to osteogenic differentiation and upregulation of osteogenic gene expression (Khatiwala et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on osteoblast differentiation.

claim: Sea urchin ROCK could be a part of the mechano-sensing mechanism that detects the high spicule stiffness and transduces it into gene expression, providing a necessary feedback between spicule elongation and the skeletogenic GRN.
source: Sea urchin ROCK could be a part of the mechano-sensing mechanism that detects the high spicule stiffness and transduces it into gene expression, providing a necessary feedback between spicule elongation and the skeletogenic GRN.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the known role of ROCK in mechanotransduction in other systems.

claim: The actomyosin network is a part of the common molecular tool-kit of biomineralization.
source: Overall, our findings together with the role of the actomyosin network in biomineralization, from calcifying and silicifying single cells to vertebrates' bones and teeth (Langer et al., 2010; Durak et al., 2017; Tyszka et al., 2019; Tesson and Hildebrand, 2010a; Tesson and Hildebrand, 2010b; Strzelecka-Kiliszek et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018; Khatiwala et al., 2009), suggest that this molecular machinery is a part of the common molecular tool-kit of biomineralization.
evidence: This is a proposed conclusion based on the integration of findings from this study and prior knowledge.

claim: Most likely, the actomyosin network was employed independently, downstream of distinct GRNs across Eukaryotes, to control mineral growth and morphogenesis.
source: Most likely, the actomyosin network was employed independently, downstream of distinct GRNs across Eukaryotes, to control mineral growth and morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary hypothesis based on the findings.
